blocks.text: Operators are the symbols that actually do something with values. They add numbers, compare them, and combine true and false. Operators are what turn stored data into real logic.

blocks.alt: Operator categories: arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment

blocks.text: If variables are the nouns of a program, operators are the verbs. Without them, your program could store values but never act on them.
You already know most operators from school maths. Programming just adds a few new ones and some rules about how they behave. This lesson makes all of them clear.
These do everyday maths on numbers. You have seen all of them before.

codes.python:
print(7 + 3)    # 10
print(7 * 3)    # 21
print(7 % 3)    # 1, the remainder after dividing

blocks.text: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication behave exactly as you expect. Division and remainder have a couple of surprises we will cover next.
The Division Gotcha
Division hides a trap for beginners. In many languages, dividing two whole numbers throws away the decimal part of the answer.

codes.python:
print(7 / 3)    # 2.333... in Python 3
print(7 // 3)   # 2, because // forces whole number division
codes.java:
System.out.println(7 / 3);      // 2, both values are ints
System.out.println(7 / 3.0);    // 2.333, one value is a double
codes.cpp:
cout << 7 / 3 << endl;      // 2, both values are ints
cout << 7 / 3.0 << endl;    // 2.333, one value is a double

blocks.text: In Java and C++, dividing two integers gives an integer, silently dropping the fraction. If you want a decimal answer, make at least one value a decimal.
If a division result is missing its decimals, the cause is almost always integer division. Convert one value to a decimal to fix it.
The remainder operator, written as %, is secretly one of the most useful tools in all of programming. It gives what is left over after division.

codes.python:
print(10 % 3)   # 1, because 10 divided by 3 leaves 1
print(12 % 4)   # 0, because 12 divides evenly by 4

blocks.text: Why it matters so much

items: Even or odd: a number is even when number % 2 equals 0.
Last digit: number % 10 gives the last digit of a number.
Cycling: index % length keeps a counter looping around a fixed range.
Divisibility: a % b equals 0 means a divides evenly by b.

blocks.text: Whenever a problem talks about even and odd, last digits, or repeating cycles, the modulo operator is very likely part of the answer.
Comparison Operators
These compare two values and always hand back a boolean, either true or false. You will lean on them constantly inside conditions and loops.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operator","Meaning"],"rows":[["==","equal to"],["!=","not equal to"],[">","greater than"],["<","less than"],[">=","greater than or equal to"],["<=","less than or equal to"]]}

codes.python:
print(5 > 3)     # True
print(5 == 5)    # True
print(5 != 5)    # False

blocks.text: This is one of the most common beginner bugs, so it deserves its own moment. A single equals sign and a double equals sign mean very different things.

items: = assigns a value: it puts something into a variable.
== compares two values: it asks whether they are equal.

codes.python:
x = 5        # assignment: put 5 into x
print(x == 5)  # comparison: is x equal to 5? True

blocks.text: Mixing up = and == is a classic bug. If a condition behaves strangely, check whether you accidentally used one equals sign where you meant two.
Logical Operators
Logical operators join true and false values so you can ask more than one question at the same time.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operator","Meaning","Example"],"rows":[["and / &&","true only when both sides are true","x > 0 and x < 10"],["or / ||","true when at least one side is true","x < 0 or x > 100"],["not / !","flips true and false","not isEmpty"]]}

codes.python:
age = 20
print(age > 18 and age < 65)   # True, both are true
print(age < 13 or age > 60)    # False, neither is true
print(not (age > 18))          # False

blocks.text: The real power comes from combining comparisons with logical operators to express rich rules.

codes.python:
temperature = 25
is_sunny = True

if temperature > 20 and is_sunny:
    print("Great day for a walk")

blocks.text: You can chain as many conditions as you need with and and or. Use brackets to make the order clear when you mix them.
Long chains of and and or can get hard to read. If a condition becomes a puzzle, give parts of it clear variable names first.
Short Circuit Evaluation
Logical operators are clever. They stop checking as soon as the answer is certain. This is called short circuit evaluation.

items: With and, if the first part is false, the whole thing is already false, so the second part is skipped.
With or, if the first part is true, the whole thing is already true, so the second part is skipped.

blocks.text: This is not just an optimisation. It lets you safely check something exists before you use it, all in one line.
Order matters with short circuiting. Put the cheap or safety check first, so the risky part only runs when it should.
Assignment operators are shortcuts for updating a variable using its own current value. They save typing and read cleanly, especially inside loops.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operator","Meaning","Same as"],"rows":[["=","assign a value","x = 5"],["+=","add, then assign","x = x + 3"],["-=","subtract, then assign","x = x minus 3"],["*=","multiply, then assign","x = x * 3"],["/=","divide, then assign","x = x / 3"]]}

codes.python:
score = 10
score += 5     # now 15
score *= 2     # now 30
print(score)   # 30

blocks.text: So score += 5 is just a shorter way of writing score = score + 5. You will see this constantly when building up totals.
Operator Precedence
When several operators appear together, the computer follows an order, just like in school maths. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction.

codes.python:
print(2 + 3 * 4)     # 14, the 3 * 4 happens first
print((2 + 3) * 4)   # 20, brackets force the addition first

blocks.text: Comparisons happen after arithmetic, and logical operators happen after comparisons. So a plus b is worked out before it is compared, and the comparison is done before and or or.
When in doubt, add brackets. They make the order obvious to the computer and to the next person reading your code.
Some operators work on text too, but they behave differently than with numbers.

codes.python:
first = "Riya"
print(first + " Sharma")   # Riya Sharma, joining text
print("ha" * 3)            # hahaha, repeating text

blocks.text: The plus sign joins two pieces of text together, which is called concatenation. The star repeats text a number of times. Neither does maths, because text is not a number.
Trying to add a number to text usually causes an error. Convert the number to text first, or the text to a number, depending on what you want.
Comparisons Produce Booleans
It is worth saying clearly: every comparison produces a boolean, a true or false value. This is the bridge between operators and decisions.

codes.python:
is_adult = age >= 18     # stores True or False
print(is_adult)

blocks.text: You can store the result of a comparison in a variable and use it later. Every if statement you ever write is really just checking one of these boolean results.

Computers store numbers as bits, meaning zeros and ones. Bitwise operators work directly on those bits. You will not need them early, but they show up in some clever DSA tricks, so it helps to know they exist.

items: and, written &, keeps a bit only when both bits are one
or, written |, keeps a bit when either bit is one
xor, written ^, keeps a bit when exactly one bit is one
shift left, written with two less than signs, moves bits up, which doubles a number
shift right, written with two greater than signs, moves bits down, which halves a number

blocks.text: Do not worry about mastering these now. Just recognise the symbols so they do not confuse you when you meet them later.
Comparing Text
Comparison operators work on text too. They compare in dictionary order, so earlier words are considered smaller.

codes.python:
print("apple" < "banana")   # True, apple comes first
print("cat" == "cat")       # True, exactly equal

blocks.text: Text comparison is usually case sensitive, so capital letters may sort before small letters. When comparing user input, you often convert both sides to the same case first.
The in operator checks whether a value is present inside a list or a piece of text. It is a clean, readable way to ask "does this contain that?".

codes.python:
print(3 in [1, 2, 3])       # True
print("a" in "cat")         # True
print("z" in "cat")         # False

blocks.text: This single operator replaces a whole loop that would otherwise check each item, so it keeps your code short and clear.

content.title: 9. Working Out an Expression Step by Step

blocks.text: Let us evaluate a mixed expression exactly the way the computer does, one step at a time.

items: First arithmetic: 3 * 4 is 12, so it becomes 2 + 12 > 10 and True
Then addition: 2 + 12 is 14, so it becomes 14 > 10 and True
Then comparison: 14 > 10 is True, so it becomes True and True
Finally the logical part: True and True is True

blocks.text: When an expression confuses you, slow down and evaluate it in this order: arithmetic, then comparisons, then logical operators. Brackets jump the queue.
The minus symbol plays two roles. It subtracts one number from another, and it also marks a number as negative.

codes.python:
x = -5          # a negative number
print(3 - -2)   # 5, three minus negative two

blocks.text: The computer works out which meaning applies from the context. You rarely need to think about it, but it explains why two minus signs in a row are allowed.
One last warning about operators. Comparing two decimal numbers for exact equality is risky, because computers cannot store some decimals perfectly.
The tiny storage error makes the two sides differ by a whisker. Instead of exact equality, check that the difference is smaller than a tiny amount.
For whole numbers, equality is always safe. It is only decimals where exact equality can betray you.

items: Using one equals sign where you meant two, mixing assignment with comparison
Forgetting that dividing two integers drops the decimals
Chaining conditions without brackets and getting the order wrong
Trying to add a number and text directly without converting
Confusing and with or, which flips the whole meaning

blocks.text: When a condition gives the wrong answer, print the individual comparisons first. Seeing each true or false quickly reveals which part is off.
What is the difference between / and // in Python?
A single slash gives a decimal answer. A double slash forces whole number division, dropping the decimals.
When would I ever use modulo?
Constantly. Checking even or odd, getting the last digit of a number, and looping an index around a fixed range all use it.
Why is my comparison always false?
Check that you used two equals signs, not one, and that you are comparing values of the same type, not a number with text.
Does and or or come first?
and is evaluated before or, much like multiplication before addition. Use brackets when you want to be sure.

items: Operator: a symbol that acts on values.
Operand: a value an operator acts on.
Modulo: the remainder after division, written %.
Boolean: a true or false value.
Precedence: the order in which operators are applied.
Concatenation: joining pieces of text together.
Read a number and print whether it is even or odd using modulo.
Read two numbers and print the larger using a comparison.
Read a number and print its last digit.
Check whether a year is a leap year using and and or.
Build a running total in a loop using the += shortcut.

blocks.text: With operators and comparisons ready, you can now make your program take decisions. That is the next lesson: conditionals.
